meta_description: Diálogo is a free declarative visual programming environment in which children build games and simulations from symbols they draw themselves. Runs offline on Windows, Mac and Linux, with a seven-session curriculum.
meta_keywords: visual programming, declarative programming, programming for kids, K-12 computing education, drawing-based programming, metaprogramming, block-based alternatives, computational thinking, games without code
og_description: A declarative visual programming environment where children draw their own symbols.
tagline: A visual programming environment where children draw their own symbols
what_p1: Diálogo is a free programming environment for children (roughly ages 10 to 17; younger kids with an adult alongside) in which programs are built from symbols the children draw themselves, rather than from predefined blocks. The language rests on two relations between symbols, substitution and categorization, plus about ten visual combinators (push, pull, teleport, collide, wildcards, an evaluation viewer). From that small set, children build games, simulations and abstract symbolic models, such as numbers and addition from scratch.
what_p2: Rules live on the same board as the game. A character can push a rule out of the way and change the program while it runs, so metaprogramming becomes something a child can see and touch. A step-by-step execution viewer shows which rule fired at each step, and doubles as the debugger.
para_chicos: Build games from your own drawings
Give characters behavior by combining a handful of visual combinators
See, step by step, why the game does what it does
Make games that rewrite their own rules while you play
para_docentes: Declarative from the first session, with no syntax and no imperative prerequisite
Runs offline on modest hardware, with no account or server; projects are saved locally
Interface in ten languages; adding one more means translating a single text file
A seven-session curriculum delivered as videos addressed to the children, so you can adopt it before mastering the paradigm

step1_p: An introduction you play in the browser, solving small challenges. It teaches the two relations the language is built on, and it needs no installation and no account.

online_note: Or try the online version: it runs the full Diálogo in the browser, with no installation, and can save your files, but it is slow and downloads about 30 MB the first time. For real use, the installed version is much better, and to simply see what Diálogo is about, the tutorial is faster.
dev_note: Diálogo is under active development. Bug reports and classroom stories are welcome at agustin@dialog.ar.
step3_p1: Each session introduces one abstraction mechanism through a playable artifact. Sessions 1 to 5 build games; sessions 6 and 7 move toward abstract symbolic models. Sessions 1 to 3 form a self-contained introduction, with a playable game already in session 2.
step3_p2: The lessons are videos addressed directly to the children. The videos are currently in Spanish; an English version is in preparation.

clases.texto: Categorization, the first mechanism of abstraction. Build a board and pieces that capture each other, then replace case-by-case rules with rules over categories.
Substitution, the second mechanism. A growing-body snake, removing duplicated code, and the execution viewer as a debugger.

clases.titulo: Session 3: From Pac-Man to a research submarine
clases.texto: A classic that puts every combinator to work, then re-skinned into a new domain. Simple rules, surprising results.
What happens when a program modifies itself? A labyrinth whose rules can be pushed and pulled during play.
Ideas from game development: event-driven rules, hidden objects, collisions and time control, all combined in one shooter.
Recursion and abstract symbol manipulation. Numbers and addition built from scratch, with no game and no character.
Modularity and reuse. Add a scoring system to an earlier game, with no variables at all.

research_intro: Diálogo is developed at the University of Buenos Aires as a research project on declarative programming for children. Both the environment and the curriculum are released as artifacts for adoption and empirical study.
paper1_note: The environment's design, its evolution across an in-person workshop and an online course, and the seven-session sequence.
paper2_note: The conceptual foundation: substitution and categorization as the two relations from which the language is built.
research_contact: Interested in using Diálogo in your classroom or your research, in translating the curriculum, or in running a study with it? Write to agustin@dc.uba.ar.
